title: The Limited Skin
prompt: Your favorite game releases a limited skin for 2,000 credits. You don't have enough. The app offers to sell you the credits for $19.99 using the debit card saved on your account.
method_guidance: This is real money buying virtual credits, which then buy a cosmetic item inside one game.
It's coming straight out of your bank balance through the saved debit card.
You're agreeing to a real charge, and probably to owning the skin only inside this one app.
Your balance drops by $19.99, permanently, even if the skin or game disappears later.
Check your actual bank balance before buying, and ask whether you'd want this without the countdown timer.

title: The First Paycheck
prompt: You worked 20 hours at $12/hour — you expected $240. Your paycheck shows direct deposit of $211.40, with lines for "Federal," "FICA," and "State."
method_guidance: This is your pay stub — a breakdown of what you earned versus what actually landed in your account.
The $240 came from your hours worked; the missing $28.60 was withheld and sent to the government, not lost.
By taking the job, you agreed to have taxes withheld automatically — this isn't optional or a mistake.
This gap between gross pay and take-home pay happens every paycheck, so budget using the deposited amount, not the hourly math.
Log into the payroll or banking app and match the deposit amount and each withholding line against your pay stub.

title: Zero Percent for Six Months
prompt: An online store offers to split your $180 sneaker order into 4 payments of $45, "0% interest, no fees." You just tap "Pay in 4" at checkout.
method_guidance: This is Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) — a short-term loan that splits one purchase into several future payments.
The store gets paid in full today by the BNPL company; you now owe that company the remaining three payments from your future money.
You're agreeing to three more automatic charges to your card on set dates, whether or not you have the money then.
If a payment fails or is late, "0% interest" can turn into late fees, and missed BNPL payments can eventually affect your credit.
Check the payment schedule and your calendar together, and confirm you'll actually have $45 available on each due date.

title: The Subscription You Forgot
prompt: You check your bank app and see $9.99 charged monthly for the last five months from an app you tried once and never opened again.
method_guidance: This is a recurring subscription — an automatic charge that repeats until someone cancels it.
Nearly $50 total has quietly come out of your checking account for something you're not using.
When you signed up, you agreed to let the app charge your card every month until you cancel.
Left alone, this keeps charging every month indefinitely — small recurring charges add up fast over a year.
Scroll through a full month of bank transactions (or the app's subscription settings) to find and cancel it directly.

title: DM from 'Instagram Support'
prompt: An account with the platform's logo as its picture messages you: "Your account will be deleted in 24 hours. Verify your identity by entering your password and card details at this link."
method_guidance: This is a phishing message — a fake "support" account impersonating the real platform to create panic.
It's not asking for money yet; it's trying to get your password and card number so it can take money later.
If you click the link and enter details, you're handing over the keys to your account and possibly your card.
Scammers can lock you out, post as you, or use your saved card for charges you never approved.
Real platforms never DM you asking for your password. Go to the app directly (not the link) to check your account status.

title: The Overdraft Text
prompt: You buy a $6 coffee with your debit card. Ten minutes later: "Your account balance is -$14.20. An overdraft fee of $35 has been applied."
method_guidance: This is an overdraft — the bank let you spend more than you had, then charged a fee for covering the gap.
The bank temporarily covered the shortfall using its own money, then billed you for that service.
By opening the account, you agreed to the bank's overdraft terms — whether that's automatic coverage with a fee, or declined transactions.
You now owe the bank $49.20 total, and further transactions could trigger more fees until the balance is fixed.
Check your account settings for overdraft protection options, and always check your real balance (not just what you think you have) before spending.

title: The Robux Reseller
prompt: A stranger on a forum offers to buy your 15,000 in-game currency for $80 cash via a payment app — "cheaper than the official store, DM me your login."
method_guidance: This is an unofficial, outside-the-game trade of virtual currency for real cash — not something the game company runs or protects.
The $80 would come from the stranger, but only after you hand over full access to your account.
Sharing your login means agreeing to trust a stranger with everything on your account, not just the currency.
The most common outcome: they take the account and never pay, and most games ban accounts caught in outside trades — you could lose everything, officially, for breaking the rules.
Check the platform's own terms of service — official in-app stores are the only verified way to convert real money and game currency.

title: The Crypto Tip from a Classmate
prompt: A classmate shows you a chart: "I put in $50 last month and it's already worth $140. You should buy in now before it goes even higher."
method_guidance: This is a cryptocurrency — a digital asset whose price moves based on what people are willing to pay for it, not a bank-set value.
Any gain your classmate has exists only on paper until they actually sell — and the money to buy it has to come from you, at today's price, whatever that is.
Buying in means agreeing to a price that can swing sharply in either direction, with no guarantee it keeps climbing.
The same coin that tripled can also drop back down fast — "it's already worth more" is not a promise about tomorrow.
Look up the asset's price history yourself on a reputable source, and never invest money you can't afford to lose based on a friend's screenshot.

title: The AI Stylist Wants Your Card
prompt: A shopping app's AI assistant says: "Based on your style, I found the perfect jacket. Should I go ahead and complete the purchase for you?" and shows a 60-second countdown before it auto-confirms.
method_guidance: This is an AI shopping agent that can complete a real purchase on your behalf, not just suggest one.
If you let it proceed, the money comes straight from your saved card or connected account, just like checking out yourself.
Confirming (or letting the timer run out) means agreeing to the price, the item, and whatever return policy applies — decided in seconds.
You could end up with something you didn't fully choose, and returning AI-driven purchases isn't always as simple as normal ones.
Turn off auto-confirm timers where possible, and always review the price and item yourself before an AI completes a purchase — don't let a countdown decide for you.

title: Debit Card or Prepaid Card?
prompt: You're opening your first card. One option links straight to a bank account you control; the other is a prepaid card you reload with cash and has a monthly fee.
method_guidance: Both are cards for spending, but one draws from a real bank account, and the other only holds whatever you've loaded onto it.
A debit card's money comes from your linked account balance; a prepaid card's money comes only from what you or a parent load onto it.
Opening either means agreeing to that provider's fees and rules — prepaid cards often charge monthly or reload fees that debit accounts don't.
A debit account tied to a real bank can build a banking history and may offer protections; a prepaid card's fees can quietly eat into your balance over time.
Read the fee schedule for each option side by side before choosing — the difference is usually in the fine print, not the plastic.
